segments.t: KTPH002Language unificationKTPH003 rewrites a snippet so that all of it is written in KTPH004oneKTPH005 programming language. Real-world admin scripts often are not: a Bash frame that pipes a heredoc into Perl, an inline KTPH000 program, a KTPH001 one-liner. Such a script has no single formatter, no single linter, and no analysis that can see across the language boundary.
KorTTY detects the mix locally — no AI request is needed to decide whether the option is offered — and only then asks a model to perform the rewrite.
A rewrite is not a redesign

The migration preserves observable behaviour and nothing else. Anything that cannot be carried over is reported back as a KTPH000noteKTPH001 instead of being dropped silently or replaced with an invented equivalent. Always read the notes and the before/after preview before you apply.
KTPH000Snippet editor → AI Code → Migrate into one language…KTPH001
Opens the migration dialog directly and shows the result as a before/after preview
KTPH000Snippet editor → AI Code → Full code analysisKTPH001

A collapsed KTPH000Language unificationKTPH001 panel; the migration then runs as the KTPH002firstKTPH003 stage of KTPH004Apply selectedKTPH005, so every improvement and hardening stage afterwards works on the migrated script
KTPH000Snippet editor → AI Code → Security CheckKTPH001
The same panel; the migration runs before the security fixes, so the fixes are written in the target language
KTPH000Terminal → Generate Workflow ScriptKTPH001, KTPH002AI SwarmKTPH003
The KTPH000Target language onlyKTPH001 check box, which forbids embedded foreign-language parts in the generated script from the start
Bash, Python, Perl, Ruby, PowerShell, Windows-CMD, AppleScript, JavaScript (Node) and Groovy.

Each target brings its own shebang, file extension and comment prefix, and the same per-language idioms the workflow-script generator uses. After a whole-script migration KorTTY also updates the snippet's KTPH000LanguageKTPH001, its file extension and its auto-detected AI skills, so the snippet is consistently the new kind of file.
Ansible is deliberately KTPH000notKTPH001 a target: turning an imperative script into a declarative playbook is a re-modelling, not a language migration.

An Azure DevOps pipeline, a GitHub Actions workflow, a GitLab CI file, a Jenkinsfile, an Ansible playbook, a Puppet manifest and a Dockerfile invoke Bash or PowerShell KTPH000by constructionKTPH001. Embedded shell is their design, not a defect, so KorTTY never reports such a document as "mixed" and never offers to migrate the document itself. Two narrower things are offered instead:

Offered only when the document's own script steps disagree — a pipeline with both KTPH000 and KTPH001 steps, a Jenkinsfile mixing KTPH002 and KTPH003. Only the KTPH006bodiesKTPH007 of those steps are rewritten. Every other line — structure, keys, indentation, display names, conditions, task invocations, comments — must come back character for character, and the step type is adjusted where the format requires it (KTPH004 instead of KTPH005). A result that changed anything outside the script steps is KTPH008discardedKTPH009, not offered. The snippet's language, file name and skills stay as they are: it is still the same pipeline.

Choosing a KTPH000Target platformKTPH001 converts the host document into another platform's schema — a Jenkinsfile into an Azure DevOps pipeline, for instance. This is KTPH002never suggested and never preselectedKTPH003: the selection starts on KTPH004UnchangedKTPH005, and only an explicit choice activates it.

The conversion is deliberately lossy. Platform semantics are not equivalent, so KorTTY carries over what has a real counterpart (triggers, agent or pool selection, variables, secrets, dependencies, artifacts, conditions) and reports everything else — approvals, environments, platform-specific tasks, matrix semantics, plugin calls — as notes you have to redo by hand. A result that is not recognisable as the requested target platform is discarded.
Dockerfiles are excluded from platform conversion in both directions: an image build recipe is not a CI pipeline.

For a plain script KorTTY looks for heredocs fed to another interpreter (KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, …), inline one-liners (KTPH003, KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007), and shell KTPH008programsKTPH009 handed to another language's process API. Matches inside comments are ignored.

KTPH000 expressions are deliberately not flagged: they are ubiquitous in shell, and treating them as a foreign language would make almost every script look mixed. A single external command call is likewise not an embedded language — it stays a plain process call after the migration too.
KTPH000The AI returned no usable script.KTPH001
The reply carried no script at all
KTPH000The AI returned an incomplete script.KTPH001
The result lost most of the program, or contains an omission marker such as “rest unchanged”
KTPH000The AI changed the document outside its script steps.KTPH001
A step unification rewrote part of the pipeline scaffold
KTPH000The result is not a valid … document.KTPH001
A platform conversion did not reach the requested target format
In every case the snippet is left untouched. Re-running with a stronger model, or with the profile picker in the preview window, is usually enough.
